automation_levers: Automated export BOL & 8-digit HTS substitution reconciler
B2B antitrust/interchange AP ledger claim packager
key_risks: CBP liquidation deadline or missing export trace defects
regulatory_notes: Execute all formal CBP drawback and protest filings through a licensed 19 CFR Part 111 customs broker or trade counsel under valid Customs Powers of Attorney and 19 CFR Part 190 recordkeeping.
Provide court-required third-party class-action filer disclosures clarifying that claimants may file directly at zero cost.

inputs: Importer authorization, importer-of-record identifiers, ACE entry and liquidation extracts, Form 7501 line detail, duty-payment evidence, and existing drawback or protest histories; commercial manifests supply leads rather than proof of eligibility.

Export bills of lading, AES/ITN records where applicable, inventory and manufacturing records, destruction documentation, transfer certificates, and evidence establishing the claimant's rights without duplicate recovery.

Broker and trade-counsel engagements, provision-specific eligibility and deadline matrix, duty-type exclusions, claimant contingency terms, and an itemized budget for historical-data extraction, evidence reconstruction, and filing.
plays.mechanism: Match ImportGenius/Panjiva shipment leads to importer-authorized ACE entry summaries, CBP Form 7501 data, and export or supervised-destruction evidence; 19 U.S.C. § 1313 generally permits recovery of up to 99% of eligible duties, taxes, and fees, subject to the selected drawback provision's matching, timing, and documentary requirements. Licensed 19 CFR Part 111 customs brokers perform reserved customs business and trade counsel handles legal positions, while the desk separates drawback from § 1514 protests, generally due within 180 days of liquidation or another protestable decision, and excludes antidumping/countervailing duties and other expressly ineligible assessments rather than treating all tariffs as recoverable. Target a 25%–35% contingency only on realized CBP Treasury refunds under contracts permitted for the service provider, with broker/counsel compensation separately structured to avoid prohibited unlicensed customs business or referral-fee sharing and with document reconstruction, filing, and professional costs disclosed separately from gross claims.
metrics: Supported collectible base: eligible paid duties, taxes, and fees multiplied by the applicable recovery percentage, less prior recoveries and unsupported amounts; report manifest-derived opportunities separately.
Cash economics: realized Treasury refunds, contingency receipts at 25%–35%, importer net recovery after disclosed costs, and desk contribution after evidence-acquisition and servicing expense.
Execution quality: percentage of claims with complete entry-to-disposition evidence, days remaining to each statutory deadline, refund realization rate, and post-payment adjustment exposure.
plays.name: Five-Year CBP ACE Duty-Drawback and Tariff-Protest Recovery Desk

platform_risks.detection_metric: Unsupported claimed dollars divided by proposed claim dollars, duplicate-entry incidence, and unresolved evidence exceptions before filing.
platform_risks.failure_mode: Manifest matching produces an apparently valuable claim that lacks eligible duties, claimant rights, or auditable export/destruction linkage.
platform_risks.fallback: Remove unsupported lines, pursue only independently timely and supportable alternatives through the broker or counsel, and stop reconstruction when expected net recovery no longer covers its cost.
platform_risks.impact: CBP denies or reduces recovery, reconstruction costs become unrecoverable, and paid accelerated drawback may require repayment with additional consequences.
platform_risks.trigger: ACE reconciliation reveals excluded assessments, substitution-rule failures, duplicate claims, missing transfer records, or an expired filing window.

workflow: 1. Obtain importer permission and reconcile manifest leads to paid ACE entries; segregate eligible duty components, potential drawback provisions, § 1514 issues, and entries already refunded, claimed, protested, or outside the relevant deadline.

2. Have the licensed broker and trade counsel validate direct-identification or substitution requirements, export/destruction timing, claimant rights, and required privileges or notices; generally track export/destruction within five years of importation and complete drawback filing within five years of export/destruction, subject to the applicable provision.

3. Build an entry-to-export or destruction evidence ledger, price unresolved documentation gaps, and submit supported claims or timely protests through the authorized professional without using a protest to bypass an expired statutory claim route.

4. Reconcile Treasury receipts, offsets, claim reductions, accelerated-payment exposure, and final liquidation; invoice the agreed percentage only against realized refunds and maintain records and reserves for audit adjustments or repayment.

inputs: Importer-authorized ACE entry-line exports, original classifications and preference claims, liquidation dates, invoices, product specifications, composition and use evidence, and actual duty payments.

Relevant CROSS decisions and their modification or revocation history, HTSUS legal notes and applicable interpretive rules, and USMCA or other FTA certifications supported by production and origin records.

Licensed-broker and trade-counsel engagements, entry-specific PSC/protest/FTA deadline calendar, prior-refund ledger, and quoted costs for technical analysis, origin substantiation, translations, and filing.
plays.mechanism: Audit import lines against the HTSUS, product specifications, CBP CROSS rulings, and agreement-specific origin evidence, recognizing that another importer's published ruling is persuasive only to the extent its facts and legal analysis fit and does not itself bind CBP for this importer. Licensed customs brokers and trade counsel select the available route: an ACE Post-Summary Correction for eligible unliquidated entries, a timely § 1514 protest for protestable liquidation errors, or a qualifying § 1520(d) post-importation preference claim generally filed within one year of importation for an agreement covered by that statute, including USMCA. The collectible base is supported historical overpayment actually refundable through the selected route, net of offsets and professional/documentation costs; prospective landed-cost savings remain a separate forecast and never count as collected refunds.
metrics: Historical recovery funnel: identified overpayment, legally reachable and evidence-supported refund base, accepted adjustments, and realized Treasury receipts after offsets.
Net recovery efficiency: collected refunds less broker, counsel, origin-documentation, and desk charges, with servicing hours and acquisition costs per recovered dollar.
Prospective performance: verified duty-rate change and realized savings on subsequent imports, reported separately from retroactive refunds and from untested volume forecasts.
plays.name: CBP CROSS HTS Reclassification, PSC and FTA Retroactive-Refund Desk

platform_risks.detection_metric: Percentage of proposed refund dollars lacking verified product facts, current legal support, origin substantiation, or a valid filing route.
platform_risks.failure_mode: A superficially similar CROSS ruling or incomplete origin certification supports an invalid refund position.
platform_risks.fallback: Withdraw unsupported positions, preserve independently valid timely claims, retain the supported classification, and obtain additional technical evidence or a prospective binding ruling before changing future treatment.
platform_risks.impact: Refunds are denied, future entries may be underpaid, and the importer incurs amendment, assessment, and professional-review costs.
platform_risks.trigger: Technical review finds materially different product facts, a revoked ruling, unmet origin requirements, or an entry outside the chosen correction or claim window.

workflow: 1. Reconcile paid entry lines to liquidation status and product facts; estimate historical overpayment separately from future import-volume savings and exclude entries with duplicate recovery or no remaining statutory route.

2. Have the broker and counsel test the proposed classification against HTSUS text, legal notes, and factually relevant CROSS rulings; verify agreement-specific origin rules rather than relying on a supplier certificate alone.

3. Submit an eligible PSC generally within 300 days of entry and at least 15 days before scheduled liquidation, whichever deadline comes first, a timely § 1514 protest where appropriate, or a complete qualifying § 1520(d) claim within its one-year importation deadline; verify current ACE restrictions and do not substitute one route for another's expired deadline.

4. Reconcile liquidation changes and actual Treasury payments to each entry, deduct agreed recovery costs, and separately implement supported classifications or seek a prospective binding ruling for future entries without counting projected savings as refund cash.

plays.name: B2B Class-Action & Antitrust Settlement Contingency Recovery
plays.mechanism: Monitor multibillion-dollar corporate antitrust and commercial class-action settlement funds (payment-card interchange, freight, auto parts, commercial insurance, SaaS) where 85–90% of eligible small businesses never file, and recover verified payouts on a 25–33% contingency fee.
inputs: Active federal B2B class-action settlement docket calendar & claims-administrator portals
B2B merchant-processing, fleet, & vendor spend intake pipeline
Contingency claim-preparation & court-authorized third-party filing agreements
workflow: Track open and upcoming commercial class-action settlements with verified court-appointed claims administrators and $50M–$5B+ settlement pools
Sign zero-upfront-cost (25–33% contingency) authorization agreements with operating restaurants, medical practices, retailers, and fleets
Extract historical merchant statements or vendor invoices, submit audited claim packages to the settlement administrator, and reconcile fee splits upon disbursement
metrics: Average gross settlement recovery per enrolled business ($5,000–$150,000+)
Claim acceptance rate by court-appointed administrator (%)
Net contingency fee per operator hour invested

platform_risks.failure_mode: Claim rejection, administrator audit hold, or court cap on third-party filer fees
platform_risks.trigger: Submitting unsubstantiated spend estimates, missing court bar dates, or failing to include required third-party filer disclosures
platform_risks.impact: Delayed payout disbursement or court-mandated fee reduction
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deficiency-notice rate (<2% target) and 100% court-approved disclosure compliance
platform_risks.fallback: File strictly for verified operating businesses with primary processor/vendor statements and use court-approved third-party claim-filing riders

plays.name: CBP "First-Sale Rule" (19 CFR § 152.103) Multi-Tier Customs Valuation Arbitrage
plays.mechanism: Restructuring multi-tiered import supply chains under the US Court of Appeals *Nissho Iwai* 'First Sale Rule' so US importers legally declare the lower factory-to-middleman transaction price ($8) for US Customs duty and tariff calculation rather than the middleman-to-US-importer invoice price ($18)—slashing annual tariff cash outflows by 35–55% across $10M–$250M+ in imported merchandise.
inputs: US Customs bill-of-lading and HTS duty-spend intelligence identifying mid-market importers paying $1M–$20M/yr in duties via trading companies
Three-party contract, factory cost-sheet, and arm's-length transfer-pricing documentation templates satisfying CBP *Nissho Iwai* criteria
Licensed customs brokerage and trade-attorney opinion pipeline
workflow: Identify US importers purchasing finished goods through Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwanese, or European trading intermediaries or sourcing agents
Audit the two-tier transaction chain to confirm (1) bona fide sale from factory to middleman, (2) clear designation for US export at factory order, and (3) arm's-length pricing
Implement compliant multi-tier invoicing and ERP documentary trails so the customs broker declares the factory's First-Sale price on CBP Form 7501 instead of the middleman's marked-up invoice
Collect a 25–35% contingency fee on all prospective and retroactive (Post-Summary Correction / Protest) duty reductions realized by the importer
metrics: Percentage reduction in declared customs dutiable value (typically 30–50%)
Annualized cash tariff savings ($300k–$5M+/yr per importer) and retroactive PSC refund recovery ($)
CBP CF-28/CF-29 Request for Information audit survival rate (100% documentary compliance)

platform_risks.failure_mode: CBP disallowance of First-Sale valuation during a CF-28 Request for Information audit
platform_risks.trigger: Related-party factory/middleman entities failing to prove arm's-length profit margins or refusing to disclose factory commercial invoices
platform_risks.impact: Re-assessment of duties on the second-sale price plus interest
platform_risks.detection_metric: Annual pre-audit verification of factory commercial invoices, bank wire proofs, and OECD transfer-pricing benchmark studies
platform_risks.fallback: Store encrypted factory invoices in a confidential customs-broker escrow vault (so the US buyer never sees the middleman's margin, while CBP auditors have full access) and back every program with a formal customs-counsel opinion letter

plays.name: Section 321 "De Minimis" & Border Bonded-Warehouse Tariff Split-Shipping Arbitrage
plays.mechanism: Routing bulk sea/air container imports for high-tariff DTC and marketplace brands into Tijuana (IMMEX) or Canadian border-zone bonded 3PL warehouses instead of US ports, then fulfilling individual US consumer orders across the border daily under 19 U.S.C. § 1321 (Section 321 Entry Type 86)—legally eliminating 15%–42.5% customs duties on qualifying consumer parcels and charging brands 35–50% of the saved tariff bill plus 3PL fulfillment fees.
inputs: USITC Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) database cross-referenced against US Customs Bill-of-Lading import records (ImportYeti / Panjiva / Datamyne)
Nearshore Mexican IMMEX or Canadian customs-bonded fulfillment center 5–15 miles from San Ysidro/Otay Mesa or Windsor/Blaine border crossings
Automated CBP ACE Entry Type 86 manifest software transmitting 10-digit HTS and consignee data per individual consumer parcel
workflow: Scrape public maritime Bill-of-Lading records to identify US apparel, footwear, luggage, and consumer-goods brands importing 20+ containers/yr in 18%–37.5% HTS duty brackets
Divert the client's ocean containers in-bond (IT/T&E bond) directly to the nearshore border-zone fulfillment facility without paying US bulk entry duties
Sync the warehouse WMS with the brand's Shopify/Amazon store so each US consumer order (<$800 retail value, 1 per person per day) is picked, packed, and cleared via CBP Entry Type 86 at $0 duty
Line-item bill the brand for standard pick-and-pack fulfillment plus a 35–50% contingency split of the verified customs duties eliminated
metrics: Annualized customs duty eliminated ($500k–$10M+/yr per enterprise brand client)
Net tariff-savings share + 3PL margin ($) per parcel cleared across the border
CBP Type 86 automated release rate (>99.4%) and border transit time (<6 hours to USPS/FedEx domestic injection)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory exclusion of specific Section 301 country-of-origin SKUs from Section 321 de minimis eligibility
platform_risks.trigger: Executive/statutory rulemaking removing China-origin Section 301 HTS codes from Entry Type 86 eligibility or tightening 10-digit HTS description rules
platform_risks.impact: Loss of Section 321 duty exemption on affected country-of-origin SKUs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Real-time HTS + Country-of-Origin eligibility screen in the WMS before container booking
platform_risks.fallback: Focus on non-301 origin goods (Vietnam, India, EU, Bangladesh, Cambodia) where high MFN duties (16%–32% on apparel/footwear/textiles) remain 100% Section 321 exempt, and pair with CBP First-Sale Valuation for remaining SKUs

inputs: Customer authorization, carrier account access through approved interfaces, invoice line items, tracking events, package dimensions and weights, and payment or credit records.
Effective carrier contracts, tariff versions, negotiated dimensional divisors, minimum-net-charge provisions, service-guarantee exclusions and claim deadlines by service and geography.
Contingency agreement specifying a 35%–50% fee on realized recoveries, treatment of existing customer disputes, and a separate methodology for compensation on negotiated prospective savings.
plays.mechanism: Audit authorized FedEx Billing Online, UPS Billing Center and DHL invoice exports against shipment events, measured dimensions and the customer's effective service agreements. Recover eligible late-delivery guarantee, dimensional-weight and duplicate-billing overcharges for a negotiated 35%–50% of realized refunds, excluding suspended guarantees, waived rights and expired claims. Separately negotiate minimum-net-charge caps or floors where the carrier offers them, measuring prospective savings against an agreed shipment-level baseline rather than treating a valid contractual minimum as an overcharge.
metrics: Realized refund yield: verified carrier credits or cash received divided by audited parcel spend, segmented by late delivery, dimensional weight and duplicate billing.
Claims acceptance and timeliness: accepted dollars divided by submitted dollars, with the percentage of eligible claims filed before the applicable deadline.
Operator contribution: collected contingency fees minus data, submission and dispute costs; report prospective minimum-charge savings separately from refunds.
plays.name: Parcel Carrier Late-Delivery, Dim-Weight and Minimum-Net-Charge Recovery Operator

platform_risks.detection_metric: Weekly rejection dollars by reason, missed-deadline count, authentication failures and credit-posting latency relative to the carrier-specific baseline.
platform_risks.failure_mode: The carrier rejects claims or restricts access because guarantee eligibility, filing rules or supported integration methods differ from the audit assumptions.
platform_risks.fallback: Pause the affected automation, use authorized exports and supported manual submission channels, and restrict recovery forecasts to confirmed eligible services and open filing windows.
platform_risks.impact: Expected recoveries disappear, processing costs rise and unsupported automation can jeopardize customer account access.
platform_risks.trigger: A guarantee suspension, contractual waiver, claim-window change, undocumented endpoint dependency or portal authentication change.

workflow: 1. Import customer-authorized exports or documented APIs, normalize tracking and invoice identifiers, and create a deadline queue without assuming every carrier provides a claims-submission API.

2. Recalculate eligible charges and delivery commitments using the applicable contract version; remove guarantee suspensions, customer-caused exceptions, duplicates already credited and claims outside their filing window.
3. Submit evidence-backed claims through permitted carrier channels, track acknowledgments and appeals, and present minimum-net-charge negotiation scenarios separately from historical billing errors.
4. Reconcile posted credits to invoices and customer receipts, invoice the agreed contingency only on realized recovery, and monitor negotiated pricing against the agreed baseline.

plays.name: Automated Parcel, LTL Freight & Tariff Overcharge Contingency Auditing
plays.mechanism: Ingest mid-market shippers' UPS/FedEx/LTL EDI billing feeds and CBP Form 7501 customs entry summaries via read-only API to programmatically flag late-delivery SLA refunds, dimensional-weight billing errors, and duty-drawback refunds on a 35–50% contingency split.
inputs: Read-only UPS/FedEx/LTL carrier billing API & EDI 210 feeds
CBP ACE Form 7501 customs entry & HTS tariff schedules
Automated carrier dispute & duty-drawback claim submission engine
workflow: Connect read-only to shipper parcel/freight portals and ingest historical and daily invoice line items
Flag guaranteed-service late deliveries, duplicate accessorial fees, residential surcharges, and eligible export duty drawbacks
Auto-file carrier credit disputes and customs drawback claims, billing the client strictly 35–50% of verified credits posted to their statement
metrics: Recovered credits as % of total annual parcel/freight spend (2–8% target)
Dispute acceptance rate by carrier/customs (%)
Monthly recurring contingency revenue per shipper account

platform_risks.failure_mode: Carrier anti-automation lockouts or GSR (Guaranteed Service Refund) waiver clauses
platform_risks.trigger: Carriers inserting GSR waiver riders into custom shipper pricing agreements or throttling automated dispute bots
platform_risks.impact: Reduction in late-delivery refund volume on waived accounts
platform_risks.detection_metric: Claim approval ratio per carrier and % of audit recovery derived from billing/dim-weight errors vs. GSR
platform_risks.fallback: Pivot audit rules toward non-waivable dimensional-weight, duplicate-charge, LTL freight class, and contract-rate benchmarking recoveries

plays.name: Private B2B Group Purchasing Organization (GPO) Umbrella & Contingent Spend-Audit Arbitrage
plays.mechanism: Pool 10,000–75,000+ seats and indirect corporate spend across hundreds of SMB member companies under authorized master GPO volume brackets through Una, OMNIA or private vertical SaaS, parcel and telecom GPOs. Pair negotiated brackets with quarter-end vendor price-floor benchmarking informed by Vendr/Tropic playbooks, targeting 3%–12% vendor-paid administrative rebates and 25%–35% contingent Year-1 shared-savings splits under no savings, no fee agreements. Eligibility, rebate bases and benchmark access must be verified; disclose dual compensation and avoid double-counting rebates in client savings.
inputs: Executed GPO member and supplier agreements defining eligible aggregated spend, volume brackets, administrative rebates and compensation disclosures
Member-authorized invoices and seat inventories plus lawfully obtained, like-for-like Vendr/Tropic-style pricing benchmarks
Contingent audit contracts defining the Year-1 savings baseline, exclusions, 25%–35% fee schedule and independent reconciliation rights
workflow: 1. Enroll eligible SMB members with written authority and aggregate verified seat demand and indirect spend without exchanging competitively sensitive data.
2. Validate GPO purchasing eligibility and negotiate supplier volume brackets using lawful quarter-end benchmarks for comparable service and commitment terms.
3. Present disclosed vendor rebates and contingent fees, secure member approval and implement authorized contract changes against an agreed savings baseline.
4. Reconcile actual Year-1 savings and vendor rebates, charge only earned shared-savings fees and audit bracket eligibility and renewal pricing.
metrics: Verified eligible seats and annual member spend within contracted GPO brackets
Realized Year-1 member savings net of contingent fees on a normalized baseline
Collected administrative rebates and shared-savings fees net of reversals

platform_risks.failure_mode: Ineligible pooled spend or disputed savings invalidates rebates and contingent fees
platform_risks.trigger: Supplier audit, volume-bracket shortfall, undisclosed dual compensation or an unsupported baseline adjustment
platform_risks.impact: Rebate clawbacks, member fee disputes and loss of supplier access
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unsupported eligible spend and disputed savings or rebates as a percentage of billed compensation
platform_risks.fallback: Suspend disputed fees, reconcile documented baselines with members and suppliers, refund unearned amounts and move affected members to eligible purchasing agreements

plays.name: Public-Record & API Intelligence
plays.mechanism: Ingest fragmented county dockets, probate registries, unclaimed property ledgers, and public APIs to surface uncontested claims or high-intent B2B triggers before manual competitors.
inputs: Court & probate dockets
State controller ledgers
Public licensing & entity APIs
workflow: Poll and normalize county/state record releases on an automated cadence
Cross-match entity/kinship/lien records and filter by minimum net fee threshold
Route verified dossiers into compliant outreach and claim execution
metrics: Cost per verified lead
Docket-to-contact latency (hours)
Net recovery / conversion rate

platform_risks.failure_mode: Portal rate-limiting or CAPTCHA gating
platform_risks.trigger: High-frequency automated polling against county or agency web portals
platform_risks.impact: Delayed lead ingestion or temporary IP block on target registry
platform_risks.detection_metric: HTTP 429/403 rate and daily record ingestion delta
platform_risks.fallback: Switch to scheduled bulk FOIA/public-record exports, official data feeds, and low-frequency cached queues

plays.name: SEC Form 8-K, Form D & C-Suite Turnover Trigger Arbitrage
plays.mechanism: Parse SEC EDGAR real-time RSS/JSON feeds for Form D (private Reg D capital raises) and Form 8-K (Item 5.02 C-suite departures, Item 1.01 material agreements, Item 2.01 M&A closings) to trigger sub-hour executive outreach before commercial databases update.
inputs: SEC EDGAR real-time Submissions API & Form D / Form 8-K XML feeds
Automated filing parser extracting raise amounts, executive names, & signatory contacts
Enterprise recruiting, specialty finance, & B2B agency deal-routing desk
workflow: Ingest SEC EDGAR filings within seconds of publication using a compliant User-Agent header (<=10 requests/second)
Extract Form D issuers raising $2M–$50M (who immediately deploy capital on hiring, growth agencies, and software) and Form 8-K executive transitions
Deliver tailored briefings to the filing officers and route warm introductions to executive search firms, enterprise software resellers, and B2B agencies
metrics: EDGAR publication-to-enrichment latency (seconds)
Form D / 8-K executive response rate vs. cold baseline (3–5x lift)
Retainer and placement referral fees generated per 100 filings

platform_risks.failure_mode: SEC EDGAR automated-access block or Reg D general-solicitation confusion
platform_risks.trigger: Exceeding SEC EDGAR's 10-requests-per-second fair-access limit or omitting the mandatory contact User-Agent header
platform_risks.impact: Temporary IP block by Akamai/SEC infrastructure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Request rate strictly <=5 req/sec with compliant User-Agent and zero HTTP 403 responses
platform_risks.fallback: Enforce token-bucket rate limiting at 5 req/sec and mirror SEC nightly bulk zip archives for historical lookbacks

plays.name: Subsidized / Developer-Tenant Multi-Inbox Cold Outbound Infrastructure
plays.mechanism: Provisioning hundreds of isolated secondary domains across subsidized Microsoft 365 developer/partner tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing, and low-cost SMTP relays—sending strictly 15–25 plain-text emails per inbox per day across 300+ free/subsidized mailboxes to deliver 150,000+ monthly B2B cold emails into primary inboxes without paying $6–$12/seat retail Google Workspace pricing.
inputs: Lookalike secondary domain portfolio with automated SPF, DKIM (2048-bit), DMARC (`p=quarantine`/`reject`), and custom tracking-free MX records
Subsidized M365 partner/developer tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing catch-alls, and distributed SMTP sending nodes
Automated peer-to-peer warmup network and master unibox reply-routing webhook
workflow: Provision 100–300 secondary sending domains and bind 2–3 mailboxes per domain via automated DNS and tenant scripts
Warm every mailbox for 14–21 days with realistic thread-depth conversations before introducing live outbound prospects
Cap daily outbound volume at <=20 zero-link, zero-tracking-pixel plain-text messages per mailbox per day to stay completely beneath ESP volume heuristics
Aggregate all prospect replies into a single unified AI-triaged inbox that books qualified B2B sales calls on pay-per-show or retainer terms
metrics: Primary-inbox placement rate (%) across Gmail and Microsoft 365 seed tests
All-in monthly infrastructure cost per 10,000 delivered plain-text emails ($)
Positive reply rate (%) and booked meetings per 1,000 prospects contacted

platform_risks.failure_mode: Tenant-wide outbound throttling or domain-footprint blacklisting (Spamhaus DBL)
platform_risks.trigger: Placing too many domains inside a single tenant, embedding tracking pixels, or exceeding 30 sends/day per mailbox
platform_risks.impact: Tenant suspension or domain-level spam-folder routing
platform_risks.detection_metric: Daily seed-list inbox placement (%) and bounce rate (<1.5% hard threshold)
platform_risks.fallback: Enforce max 2–3 domains per tenant, strip all open/click tracking pixels, verify 100% of leads via SMTP catch-all checks before sending, and keep hot-standby warmed domains ready for instant swap

Qualify budget and timeline inside a 3-message DM micro-funnel and transition immediately to a booked call, checkout link, or owned SMS/email list

DM reply-to-qualified-conversation %
Revenue per 100 DM threads
